segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: It was made out of bone. And you couldn't very well lure them. Because they were... They were real bone die. They had cut the corners off too. They were doing a lot of things here in Potlatch too. And on way up there… they were..… wood legend and gambling and doing everything. Italians were wood legend, not the Greeks. The Greeks, they didn't ever dig wood. Wood like because they didn't have no places of their own, you see. Up the hallway... Now one Italian was here and was wood legend, but the... The others were up the hallway. And they were doing it there because it was a different town, you see.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you say places of their own, what do you mean? A place, a house to live in that was out of town?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Not out of town, up down way. You know, around... But not in Potlatch. Well, in Potlatch too, but not very much… in Potlatch… because they were... They didn't arrest it. They had some wine and drinking wine for themselves. And it used to come from... From Moscow, you know. The sheriff used to come around and raid in Moscow.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was that Summerfield?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yeah, Summerfield. I've heard about him.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You remember him?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: You don't remember him. No, he's dead. He's been dead for a long time. But I know Hap Moody. He was one of that bunch. Yeah, yeah. Hap Moody is in the home now.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Is he?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yeah, that's all right. He's 90 years old. Hap, he said, I know him pretty well. He's a good fellow. He's pretty smart. Pretty smart..… what you call..… and not a big fellow sheriff. He just died here not very long ago.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Jordan?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Jordan… well, I've heard about Summerfield stopping a lot of people, but not about arrests. I don't hear about many arrests. No, they didn't arrest him. They just warned him and scared him out. And how is this fellow that we had here before? He went down here once in a while. He lost.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: The last year?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No… no, he died. He was sick, you know, and he passed away just lately.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, you mean Jordan?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No, not Jordan… after Jordan.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I don't know. It's not Summerfield. You're thinking of more recent.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No, not Summerfield. He was just recently. He used to come over here with Bob Felton.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You know now?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No, I don't know the name, but I know who you mean. Felton is a lawyer, you see. Yeah. I think he's prosecuting a attorney now, isn't he… no,… now that Lérygé was, but now it's... Well, Lérygé is out. He used to fight with them, what you call the commissioners. But he didn't run. He didn't run the last time, you see. He didn't... And I think... I think Felton is prosecuting a attorney. If I remember, I don't know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: This guy that's prosecuting attorney now, he has a beard. I know that. He's a pretty young fellow.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Is he?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Yeah, the one who was prosecuting attorney for the county.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: What is his name?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I can't think of it. But you say the Greeks didn't bootleg and that was because they didn't have their own homes?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No, they didn't have their own home. But the Italians, one of the federal fellows that had family too, you see. Mike Petruolo, he used to be one of the ones who used to bootleg. He was arrested even in the jail for comforting the ones. But... He had his own place, his own family. He was selling groceries too, you see. He was backing bread too himself. And... solid. Was... No, the Greeks didn't have no... They never did bootleg. Very... One, he used to bring bottles of beer from Spokane. And he was selling once in a while, but not in a... Good high-scale, not in a big scale.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would people buy from the same bootlegger all the time if they could? Or would they buy just from wherever they could get it?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: They could sell whatever they could get it if they wanted to. They didn't care who they buy it from. But they knew who was handling that stuff, you see. And they went over there to them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Wasn't some of it a lot better than others?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: I heard some of it was pretty bad, some of it was really good. As far as quality, how good it was… oh, the quality… the..… oh, different lot. Yeah, you mean... Yeah. Well, different... Some of it was good, and some of it was not good. What the heck is that?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Sounds like he's across the... The way here.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: The Donca here, he wants it one.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I've heard that in Spokane they had a lot of houses, too, a prostitution there.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, prostitution, yes.It was wide open in Spokane at one time. But now, I don't think they are, because I've never been in Spokane now for years. I go in for business, you know, in and out. I don't know anything about it, but... Because I used to go now for the eyes, you see how these girls walk in. And Reverend Anderson took me up there, and he means... His wife, Drog, he can drive himself. He can drive around town here, but not in Spokane. His wife is a good driver. And I used to go with him. I took a few trips for the fire pressure. And I didn't have good luck.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where was the place that you gambled? Was that Durkin's or was that some other place? I heard of a place called Durkin's up there. Is that where people gambled?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Not only one place. They were wide open. All the saloons had a lot of places on gambling. They were tablets, you know. But they even now, or lately, they had... They allowed gambling in some places. But I don't think they do now. Because I don't know. I don't know what they do now. Well, I'm more curious about the early days.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When they had prostitution, would the girls just come down in the saloons? Is that where they'd pick up the men?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, no… no, no, they were in certain places. Oh, houses, yeah. Yeah, sure. They did around in the street. Oh, there are some out in the street, too, but not too many.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Is it true that they used to come down into this area from Spokane?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Sometimes. Sometimes… sometimes, fellas, you know, that knew them. They'd bring you over here. Here was a lot of people living here, you see. Now it's dead. They had thrown two ships over there, and they were on the machinery. It took place of people, now, of men. And there are not very many men. They used to work a thousand or more, fifteen hundred people, you see. They had another street here, where we lived. Greeks and Italians. They called it the International Street. But they took them houses during the war. And because there was no, nobody to random, you see. And one fella, he's still living here. He took a contract and he hauled them away, and sold them for whatever he did. They didn't want to burn them down, you see.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was the working day? Was it a ten hour day when you were first here?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yes, ten hours a day, up to when we had that wobbly strike, whatever they called that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: The IWW, huh?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: IWW.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did that do?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, after that, that didn't do very much, no, because it didn't last very long. They formed the Law of the Legion of Loggers and Lumberman. And everybody joined up, you see. And gradually, they brought the eight hour work.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Who got?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Pretty soon, from the eight hour work. Before that, we just go down there half an hour earlier to go on the machine. You see, those ones that had the machine thrown, they had to all of themselves. And after that, why they had a man to go on, you didn't have to do anything except on a husher of blue. You were ready to go to work and ready to get out on a machine at four o 'clock. They had different business. It was strictly eight hours work. But ten hours, we worked for ten hours there for two dollars a day.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Two dollars a day?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yeah, I worked for two dollars a day here. But there were dollars. You see, three dollars you could buy a pair of shoes. But now you can't do that. You see, the dollar was worth something.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: With this ten hour a day, did you ever have overtime besides?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No, you couldn't… they didn't have no overtime on that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did it have you worked?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Because they were working ten hours, you know, and you couldn't very well have overtime to work for thirteen hours. Unless, in some places, you probably worked during the holidays, in the cold winter months, on the machinery, froze. Now there we had about half a day in Thanksgiving Day and half a day sometimes in Christmas. To keep the thing running, you see, keep it from freezing.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You mean it would freeze up if it wasn't used?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yes, it would. Sure, the machinery, yes. Now they are freezing. They had conveyors, you know, with chains. And pretty soon if it was frozen, or as soon as you started when it was frozen, they crystallized and they broke. They had trouble with that. Now they had different machinery, you see, they are all machinery. They had machinery, they had a burner here. Or they burned the west things that they didn't want to use, you see, slabs and things like that. Well, they had trouble with that because it was clear outside, you see. The conveyor was in open and that will once in a while, it will break and they have to fix it. It was different altogether. And now it's different altogether down there, even now. Because I haven't been down there for close to 20 years, you see, I've retired. And I don't know very much about it, but...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You haven't been down to visit it or see what it's like?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, I've been down a couple of times in the early days. That is after I retired, but since then I... I get down there and look. I went down there and I had... Somebody from Greece came over here and I took him down there to show him. And I had to go down, but it wasn't much change then, you see. But now they... It's a lot of changes. It's unbelievable to me. What it was, three men. It's only one man and he's got a buttons. You've been down there in the mill?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I've been at Bennett's, but I've never been here at Potlatch to see the mill.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: You haven't?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: No, I've seen the Bennett mill in Princeton.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: That's smaller. Well, that's all right. That's modern mill. That's more modern than this, I think. Because they just built that. Bennett built them… they had..… what was his name? Boone. And since Bennett took it over, he remodeled it. You know, it's where that man there, the head saw it. He's only on any punch buttons.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you worked a ten hour day, did you have to work all ten hours? Could you take breaks easily or what?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No… unless you had to go to toilet or something like that. Otherwise you work straight ten hours. But they couldn't stop you from that. They had a man. They had a man that was cleaning up, you know, and he took your place. But he couldn't take... He couldn't take everybody's place. It was a little bit different then. They had two, three men cleaning up. Now they don't have anybody, you see. The whistle blows and you go to smoke. They allow you ten minutes for a coffee break… that's all… and you have to be there when... You notice the whistle when they blow sometimes. During two o 'clock hour, two o 'clock and two, ten minutes after two, you have to be there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, did they supervise you very closely? Watch what the men did pretty close?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, not very close. The foreman was a little bit different man. You see, he washed him, yes, because some of the fellas, you know, they lay down. You know, they loosen up on their work, you see. They didn't do their work as they should be. But he couldn't watch everybody. The foreman was the whole thing then. He could fire and hire, but now he can. You know, the fireman has to go to... The man that will fire, he goes to the union and complain and they have to put him back or find out the reason why he is fired. See, they have different...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, was that a good way of doing it for the foreman to fire and hire whenever you wanted?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: It was a good and bad because if the foreman had a friend, you know, he never fired him. He fired somebody else. But then he fired him and put somebody else that is friendly to the foreman. And that way is no good, but the union, I think, is better. Although I never did join the union when I was here while I was working.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Why not?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, there was different things. There were many things that... I joined the union on the first come, the AFL, and then came the CIO and they got the bargaining agency and they wanted me to join that. And I said, no, I didn't join that because I enjoyed the AFL and they lost out. But now, of course, it's a combined AFL and CIO and everything is peaceful. At that time, they were fighting one another.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: The AFL and the CIO fought each other? Did you think the AFL was better or did it make a difference? I mean in those days.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, in those days, the AFL came first, you see, and I joined them. And then they lost the bargaining agency and they wanted me to join the CIO and I didn't.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did you think of the IWW?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Oh, well, the IWW was a radical organization anyway. It didn't last very long. It was too radical to exist. They were fighting against the capital, you see, and you can do that because the mail here, the IWW, they have to strike and get somebody to work there because they have to run, I mean.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Because they have to what?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: They have to run the sawmill, you see. They didn't want to get some of Ed Musso's talk. Did you get some of Ed Musso's?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I'm going to. Next time I see him, when I come back, see him. His wife is a very nice person, too, interesting person, too.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yeah, she's not...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: That they were, when you say against capital, the IWW, what do you mean they were, what is that?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No, ... they were against the capitalism because they were trying to do the things that they wanted to do, you see, and that was too much. They demanded a lot from the capital. And the capitalists, of course, they didn't do, they couldn't stand for that. Now it's different because they both agree to some things. They don't always agree, but they have a contract. They sign a contract and they have to abide by the agreement of the contract, whatever they do. It's different altogether. And at that time they didn't have no contract. They didn't know nothing. The IWW organized it first. And they wanted to, I never did join the IWW. I don't know very much about it. But they did try to shut the mill down in Elk River, over there, and they run them out and they told them they either have to go to work or go to an army. That was before World War I. And some did go to army. But others, they left, they built. I know one Greek fellow there that he wasn't, he didn't go to either army or anything, but he even changed his name, you know, and then they couldn't, you know, they couldn't find nothing against him.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did he try to do anything else? He just joined the strike?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, he wasn't, he wasn't the leader. And the leader went to the army. And of course after he came over, the army, he started business in gambling house in Spokane. And his son, he was general manager of the horses, who are the guardians of Spokane, George Manos. But I saw him holding the radio the other day, or he retired from that position and he's got something else now.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Is the father dead now?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you know him?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Oh yeah. I knew him.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What, he believed in the IWW then?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, he was IWW. Then after IWW was defunct, there was nothing, then he didn't care anything about IWW because he opened a gambling house and he had other business, other business than working.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What kind of a guy was he?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, he was a good man… my son… but he was a businessman. He was a friend of yours. He pretended to be a friend. And he was a friend to a certain extent. But then when it's, if he could, he would take the money away from you. He was a pretty good card player.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I thought the IWWs would be against businessmen, in the big business anyway.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: At that time it wasn't at the big business, but they were in a big business.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You mean in a business, what do they employ?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: A lot of people. Well, yeah, that's all right. But that place didn't employ very many. It was just gambling joint.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, do you think?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No, IWW was in existence then anyway, you see, after the war. And before the war, when all the existence joined the Royal Legion of Lords and Lumberman.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you think they were, what they wanted was good? The IWW?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: They wanted a little bit too much. The company wasn't ready to give it to them. Now it's different. Now they sign a contract and they have to abide by the contract. But it isn't as strong as the IWW.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was the Royal Legion of Loggers and Lumberman, was that a good union?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, it was mostly for the company. You know, it was to keep from starting and things like that. The IWW, the Loggers and Lumberman, is the predecessor of the AFML. You see, after that was defunct. The AFML came in and they signed up a lot of people here.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you think the company would have come around and given the eight-hour day and improved conditions unless the unions pushed them?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Oh, well, I don't think so. No, the company wouldn't do that. But the unions did do some pushing. The company wouldn't do that, no. Because they weren't meant to work ten hours so they can produce more lumber with cheaper wedges. But after they got the eight-hour work-wide, they had to raise their wedges too. To some extent. And now the AFML is not as bad as when they first organized. They both affiliated with the AFML and the CIO. And that way they worked better. I think one is not against the other. And they're both working together against the company of large employers. You see, the small employers like the automobile industry and so on.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you worked ten hours a day, was that very hard to do?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, at that time I was a young man. I didn't care. It wasn't very hard for me, you know. But now, of course, it will be too hard.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I wouldn't like to work ten hours a day now.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Neither would I, but I did. It was ten hours all over. You work in railroad ten hours. And railroad was worse than the sawmill, you see. Pick and so on. You had to work much a heck.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Like a what?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, you had to do the job, you see, to work pretty hard. And the boss was right there watching you. Railroad was hard work at that time, ten hours a day. And hot weather. So one time we worked down to Snake River, down to Walla Walla and Walla Walla and Umatilla down through there. It was pretty hot in summertime. But that time I was 17, 18 years old. I didn't mind it so much.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you have any way to get in out of the heat? Is there any place to go?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No, no other place, no. But of course, when I came to sawmill here, after five years after that, I stayed with it. I thought it was a better job here anyway and better wedges. A little better, not very much. But common labor here was two dollars, and in railroads was a dollar seventy-five, a dollar and a half. And how did it work? And the shift from one place to the other, you know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You told me before that the bosses looked down on the men and the railroad work. What way did they do that? Did you know that they looked down?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, I'll tell you, the boss at that time had an interpreter, because he couldn't tell me to do something and I don't understand him, you see. And of course the interpreter explained it to me. Now he will tell the interpreter that I want that dog, such a thing. And he would come over there and tell the men in their own language what to do, what the boss wanted to do. But the boss was right there all the time.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was that what you mean by he looked down at you?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: I'm not sure. That's what I mean, yes. He was watching whether you work or not. And if you don't work, he doesn't tell you anything. He tells me, he tells me because you don't understand. Oh, yeah, these are hard days, them days, on railroad and everywhere else. But them days are gone… yeah… for the present generation.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Those bosses, do you think they were, those bosses, were they fair or did they expect too much?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No, they were not fair because they had to do, the more they did, you see, the better credit they get from the company. And now maybe they would advance. They get raised or they get a better job. And that was the, they make you work hard so they get the credit that they did. And some of them, of course, they were naturally devils. They were just hard men. He says, one boss down in California, he says, I want to see one Greek to die on the trudge from working. He was a, I don't know what the heck was his name, I can't remember now. Anyway, he was pretty rough. I never worked in California myself, but that's what some of the fellows that came up from California was telling us.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What would guys do? Would they work for a man like that if he's trying to kill you?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Not exactly to kill you, but he'll work you to death, you see. I like to see one Greek die on the trudge. They were working, they were doing, yeah, well, they had to work because they couldn't do nothing else. And they had to work because if they didn't work, they didn't get paid. And they were hungry.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What made that work harder than the sawmill work? Why was it that much harder?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, because there's a fish over in the pig. You had to show it down, you see, from the trudge, from the inside of the trudge, you had to throw it out. And then the razor tried to put it under the tiles. And the railroad in the history knew. You had to put a lot of gravel on in order to keep them even. And it was to keep them even and to keep them steady, to stay, you see, when the train goes by there, it won't sink. If the ground is soft, the railroad will sink and the train will go out of the trudge. And if that happened, then it's damaging. My horse somebody, and if it's passenger train, they probably hold too many. And the company has to pay the damages. So they had to wait. It was different. But now the railroads, they don't know the railroad business. And then they were the chief industry.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You mentioned something to me about you had to work in a mudslide once… what was that?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Oh, yeah… that was in, you know where Leavenworth Washington is? It was up in the Cascades, in the mountains. They had a big slide. So the whole mountain came down there, and you had to throw the mud and everything out. And sometimes you had to keep putting in a new truck. And they come up and got me and the other fellas from the section. You see, you were working in a section. And they didn't tell us where they're going and what is wrong or anything, because we don't understand them. We did tell us anyway. But they took us over there, and the fellas, they had a car that was, the cook was there cooking. We got not to eat all right, but we didn't have nothing to wear there. We have nothing but shoes, just a pair of shoes. And we got in a mud up to the knees. We just put it off and work all night. The next morning, I don't know, I guess we stayed one night and one day. And they cleaned it up. They cleaned some of it, and then the other, so the scraper, you know, and the other machinery that they had there. And took over and we left, went back to the section. But the work train came by there and picked every section up. They said, come on.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: I think the head of a train was off the tracks too. One train, it wasn't that time though. They had one train went off the tracks and down to the river. I heard then it was before that though. And that's what they were afraid of, you see. Maybe they would call the train to go down. But at that time there was no train anyway. The train was probably away from the slide anyway. They had to stop… and they had a, well, they communicated with the depot, the depot agents and tell them that the start is a slide before they, in a certain place and they had to stop. Until they fixed it or they had to go back and get another way, go through different, you know, that was the great north. And maybe they could, no, that was the,… yeah, and go through the NP. If they could, sometimes they do that. When they have a slide or they have broken rails or something, or big like a train or they can, they take the other line. They have all these agreement.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: I don't know what they do now. I guess they do the same thing. But there's not very many passenger trains anywhere. And at that time it was everything going by train, even the mail. They had a mail train… just for mail… four fire cars, mail cars. Mail train and everything stopped letting go.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You mentioned to me that the men, most of the men couldn't save much money from those wages on the...

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Not very much, no. Not very much. But didn't you come, most of the people come over to make money so they could... But if they couldn't make what they could do, they have to take whatever they can give, whatever they can get. You know, it's a... a matter of finding jobs sometimes, too. It was a job. Sometimes we're scarce, especially in the wintertime where you couldn't do very much out in the trash. But they always did have something in railroads. And they kept our three four men in each section. Sections, railroads divided in sections, you see. We had sections over probably six, seven miles.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Six, seven miles?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yeah… and we... It was our responsibility to keep it in shape. And then another six, seven miles is another form, another section. But now they have more than six, seven miles. Now they probably have two, three sections in this line. And at that time they have seven or eight. Now they got one in pollution, one mine in puddlers. And one in a Bovill, maybe three sections. Because then they had hand cars to go to work and back, pump it by...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You know what hand car is? Have you seen one? They don't have them now, do they?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No… but I've seen... maybe it's just pictures, but I've seen them, you know, maybe in the movies, pump. Oh, yeah, that's what we had. Hand cars. They didn't have the machine, the gas lane, you know, to... now they're on by... get gas.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were the section foremen better to work for than the railroad foremen?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, they're all the same. Section foremen, some were nice fellows and some were not… you see… some section men was... when we worked one time in... in wintertime, we couldn't do very much. We just get out there and... Just enough to be out there is part sometimes where you watch... watch the... truck there and maybe broken rail or something like that, you know, we'll go over. We didn't do very much in winter because that section was all fixed in summertime. And in wintertime, there's too many in each section, you see. Just for... and of course, where I was, they had a... We had to... put up the lamps for the switches. You know, they had oil... oil lamps. They put on the switches. They were red and green. Every time you turn the switch open, you turn red. And when you cross it, it turns green. It's... okay to go... for the train to go ahead.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: And we had to take care of them. Both... both ends.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you think..… do you think most of the men were disappointed that they couldn't get better job, make more money?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Oh, well, that is natural for everybody. You know, you'll be disappointed if you can. But... they were sorry... some were very sorry for what they were getting. You know, they had to be... because they couldn't get anything else. And they could talk in the language. That's not in the house they killed there. And... they... they had to be satisfied. They couldn't... speak English and they couldn't get a job… our reason..… for us... that we stayed in section was that it kept us there... to watch the... line. And of course I couldn't understand a little bit English and... not very much, but... young men, you know. I can... speak a few words. And some of the older fathers, they couldn't speak one word. Maybe I could understand what the boss wanted, you see. Some of the bosses, they had... they had a lot of... a lot of...

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: passions… some of them... intersections because they... they had to show you what to... and if you couldn't understand... they had to make you understand by motions, you see… and..… it was pretty..… pretty hard.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: There was no interpreter in the sections?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No. Too small. The crew was too small. No, the crew was two men or four men. Or I was there, it was four men because... there was two sections. One was going east, the other was west. And six miles each way. Or six or ten miles, I don't know now, I don't remember.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Same place as the men did?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: They had a section house for the foreman and for the men. Some foreman who were married men, they had families… they couldn't..… and one foreman on a double section there, they only had one... section house and he had to stay at the hotel. There was one place there that there was... one hotel, one grocery and... section house and statue… the depot… and maybe a few... few farm... farmers..… around there… you know, it was... isolated place. Then the name of that place was... Adrian. On the... I don't think that exists anymore.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Is that Washington?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No… yeah, yeah, it was in Washington. Yeah, it was in... a freighter was about ten miles from there. West, we're in east. And I don't know that... in South Plate, there was only one hotel. And it was open in the summertime only. And nothing else. But now they tell me that it's a big town there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, did you..… you guys slept in the section house? Was that very good? Were the lodgings pretty good there?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Oh, well, we had our own bedding, you know… we had to..… use our own bedding. They didn't have no bedding or anything. We had to build our own bunks and everything else. In some sections, they had... other fellows had built them, you know. But in others, we had to build our own.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was the section house then? Was it just a bunk house?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: That's all it was?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: That's all… but it was... in the wintertime, we had a stall there, you know, and we kept the room… only one room..… house… there was a... not very... no... no water in. We did the water from outside. Even the section... even the Foreman's house was without the water. They had to get the water out in your pump.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was the Foreman's house just for one man and his family or for a lot of...

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yeah, family. Leave that to one family. They're your family. But... I don't know how they got along all right, I guess. They had to because that... situation existed all over. Like the farmhouses. They didn't have nothing, no water inside or they were not modern like they are now. All they had was... place to stay, to sleep and to cook and so on. And the water was outside. They didn't have the water piped in into the house at that time. 50 years ago or more... no, 60, 70... 60 years ago… no… i'm 60 years here. I'm 60 years in Potlatch. Even more. And five years... yeah, about 65 years I think. 65 years ago.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Could you guys go to town during the winter?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No… well, we could go to town if we get the... let us have the speed of the car, the hand car. We had to pump the car and go to town… but..… we did go to town once in a while. If we had something to buy because they didn't have everything in that little store over there, you see. There was one store with one man, one man with a great big mustache over there. And he had enough there for all we needed, you know. I don't remember whether there was a meat market there or not… but..… i think we were given the meat maybe from... Orofino once a week. And in one place, now snack here, we could get no meat or anything. You see, we could get the meat but it spoiled before Orofino was so hot, you know. But you couldn't use it. You probably could use it once, it's all. And we had to use ham or potatoes and something else, whatever we had. No meat. No fresh meat, you know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: If you went into town, did people feel out of place in a small town because they couldn't speak English?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yeah. They did… they look up on us, you know, like, yeah. Well, they knew that you couldn't speak English. One fella there, he was a gang of men, about 30 men. And he went over there to the foreman and he asked me if he'd speak English. I guess so. He thought about one of us, you know. I remember putting clearly, I guess so. And they start talking to him. Oh, it was a... Well, it was pretty...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would they try to communicate with you or did they people ignore you?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, they ignore you mostly because they knew that you could speak English, you see. And you avoid them too. Because you can talk to them. Even here in the mill, when I first came here in the mill, the fellas, you know, that we could communicate better by science than we could by talking. She's a lady with white hair and a pink dress and she's taking some stuff off her line. Oh, yeah, it's never here.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, what was these interpreters that what they did, were they very helpful or did they take advantage of the men? What were they like? In their advantage?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: They were men like us, you know. They needed to take no advantage of anything. Their job was to interpret the language. They thought that they were somebody because they could speak a few words English, but in other words, they were all right. They interpreted from the same town back in Greece. He was from the same town, you see. He came from the same place and we knew him well. He was here for a few years before. We did and he could speak a few words, maybe some of them interpreted. Maybe they could fully understand what the boss told them anyway. There was a Mario Hamasenou.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, this man who was the interpreter from your hometown, how did you hook up with him?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Oh, they were by corresponding. We were in Spokane, you see. They all got together. They were there in the employment offices there. They wanted a gang of men for so many, so many, 30 men or 40 men for a certain place in an office. Then you go there and you ask him if his job is open, okay. Of course, he was the interpreter. There was others, too. He took the job and the men to work. If we went there and didn't like it, we quit the job and go someplace else. Not always, but if the boss was some book in here. If the boss was pretty rough, you know, you want too much work, you get together there and tell him that you either have to cut down, slow down a bit or we quit. Sometimes we did quit. Go someplace else. Depending on how the work was, you know, there was plenty of work. If there wasn't, we had to stick with it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Could the boss threaten to fire the crew, too? Did he ever do that?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No. Say, if you don't work harder, I'm going to fire you. No, they didn't do that. They did try to fire some at one time. They all got together, you see, and they said, fire him or we will go. See, we got stuck together, mostly. Unless the man was worthless, he wasn't worthy of his company, then they let him go. Because they couldn't lose their own job for the sake of one man.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You did stick up for each other, though?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Oh, yes, mostly.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Now, what part of the group that you worked with on the railroads, what part of them came from? Didi Ma, from your hometown? What part of them came from your town of the whole crew?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Most of them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Most of them? How did it happen that all the folks from your hometown stuck together like that?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: We did stuck together because we had a weekend in Spokane. We knew this interpreter and we asked him that you would take us to find work for us and we all got together. Then he looked around in the employment offices for the wanted men. That way it worked all right. Of course, maybe there were few from other places that we knew them and we just take them through. But most of them were from some outfit, I mean from some town. One time, I decided to stay away from the Greeks altogether and I got a job on the bull run. You know what bull run is?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Near Portland?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yes. I got a job in contract construction work. They were building a dam, a pipeline for war for them. I stayed there, I don't know how long… i don't remember… but I was all alone. I didn't have no Greek or anybody, all Americans. Then we had a boarding house there, of course, and everything else. I stayed there for quite a while. The boss one time, he asked me, he says, what nationality you are. I told him I was a Greek. I said, I thought you were Scandinavian. I said, no. Because he didn't have no, there was no Greek, light-headed, you know. My hair was light then, you know, hair-to-hair, and I wasn't bald. He says, I thought you were Scandinavian. I said, no. But I could talk a few words, English, you see. And I said, I'm going to try and go over the Americans to learn to talk English language. And of course, there were some Mexicans there too.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How well did you get by there?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: I got by all right. I wasn't speaking too much. Somebody started to talk to me. I answered where I could. And so I didn't say too long, I think it was about three or four months.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Could you make friends in a place like that?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No… no, I couldn't because I didn't talk very much… i couldn't… i couldn't talk very much, and I was kind of staying behind, you see, staying alone. And that got a little bit too long, so it was all right while I was working because I was working almost alone. One, I had a job. They had big ballers there, you know, when the ditch was built. And the crane or the shovel that they had there, it wasn't lifted, it was too heavy. And I had a... They call them single jack.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You know what single jack is?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: It's a hammer. Yeah, a hammer and...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Chisel?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: And not chisel, but... I don't know where it was now… drill… hammer and drill and drill holes in them. There, and they blast them for a dynamite in them and blast them, you know, in the pieces, and then they haul them away with the shovel, steam shovel.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So in the evening when you weren't working is when you got lonesome?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yeah, well, I wasn't very... And I didn't... I didn't... They did one, you know, that could be friendly. They speak to you for a while, and if you find out that they don't... that you don't speak very good English or you don't understand them, well, they leave you alone. You see how it is? And that way, you can... Or some of them, they do... they call them speak to you, you know, but they're not... not to carry on the conversation for too long… so I quit… you seem to be very well posted in geography. I see that you understand, you know, where Bull Run was. Did you work around there?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I lived in Portland for a while. I know... I know Portland is pretty good. The country around there. Well, you know, that's where they get the main water for Portland now, is from Bull Run. That's the main water supply for the city. So you must have been working on putting that supply in. They put in a big reservoir and the pipe goes all the way into the city.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: What maybe?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: They close that area off. They don't let people in there because they're afraid of a fire would ruin the watershed in the summer.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, they're really pipeline there for some reason. I don't know. I think that must have been for the city of Portland. Well, maybe. It's not too far from the city. No. No. Well, I can remember, but it's close. Not too far.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I just was curious about why did you decide to leave the people that you knew in the first place? You got tired?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No, just try to be alone once in a while and see what will happen. I just, you know, I just tried to go alone and see how it's like to be among Americans. And of course, I have a pretty good job there. They didn't bother me very much. I was doing more work. I was pounding that single jack that would be the bend.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You mean you did more work than most of them did?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Heavier work?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yes and no. Well, yes. Oh, I did a lot of work. I wrote the skipper and everything else. She meant work.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What's that? Wrote the skipper?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Was that..… yeah, in construction work, you know, we had skippers and they filled them with a dart. And they were meant to ride over and unhook them to dump the work, to dump the... ...contents the dart. And I was writing that as soon as we filled it up, I grabbed the chain over there and went on. And in cement work too. But the cement, the header... ...drop... ...or dump the cement, they opened that... ...carrier, you know, big... big scoop. And I dumped it. I worked as a single man too. Signal, press a button. And one time I made a mistake and he come down and bought me out. Oh boy, that fella was..… he was mad… well, I didn't tell him anything because I couldn't stop talking. He was pointing the finger. I have no sense.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: With the signal, how you gave... What you did wrong, that the man got mad at you? You said the foreman got mad because he gave the wrong signal.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Oh yeah, well I didn't... I don't remember. I don't remember but I did give him the wrong signal, you know. And he was putting me... making... have an accident, you see. And he came down on the shaft over the whole feet. He came down there and he shook the hand, his finger, you know, at me. I didn't understand. He was telling me, well, he was... he was putting down meth. I know that. But I didn't say nothing to him anyway and he didn't dare... ...hit me because he was... oh man, but my size and I don't know if he... hit me or probably hit him bigger.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But you didn't know what you did wrong even then?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: I... I... I forgot. There was something... You knew then what it was. Oh yeah, sure. Sure, and I didn't know enough to... apologize to him, you see. I didn't... I couldn't talk to... enough to... quiet him down, you know. So... I said, yeah, I couldn't apologize to him and I said, but... but I didn't know so... I was just letting go like that. I was pretty careful the next time. Oh yeah, I won't go over. I was going to see man works... building a dam down Portland. You know who River Mill is?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I don't think so. Is it..… near Portland?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yeah… i see..… we build a dam there... at River Mill. That's the Portland... Portland Light and Power Company. Oh, okay. There's another dam... up there, but I can't remember… casadero… you know who that is?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: No, but I've heard the name. Were most of these jobs... were there other... other friends of yours along with you?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Other... they are... one called my mind. And I... we worked together... in all these similar ways. And other gigs... there were lots of gigs from different places, you know. We know them, but we got acquainted when we got there. But it wasn't the old group from... No, no, from the railroad there, no.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What happened? Did you work on railroad the first few years?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: First five years.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And then after that you did other work? Is that it?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Between the five years I worked on the railroad and on cement. And after five years I came to Potlatch in the United States… you see… five years past over there. And the River Mill is... it's closer to Portland than... And kind of painted them over, you see. And they kept... I don't know how many... they kept something. But after it was all through, we... Got laid off. Well, was... was any...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: were any of these jobs much higher paying than the railroad?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: These were good paying jobs. Sure, all of them. Yeah… i worked in...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: White Salmon, you know who White Salmon is?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yeah. Cross River from Wood River. I worked in that... damn..… hi!

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You got company again?

segments.speaker: Unknown Speaker
segments.words: No, I just come over to...

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Oh, it's no company. It's no company. It's...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Just one of the everyday people, isn't it?

segments.speaker: Unknown Speaker
segments.words: Look at the flies on the outside of the screen. They're trying to get in. What the heck have you got here?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Look at all this. Did the crew... was the old crew from your hometowns?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No, I...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did they still work on the railroad?

segments.speaker: Unknown Speaker
segments.words: No, I lived exactly on the... I was in different... Oh, yes. Goodbye.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yeah, goodbye.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You gonna bring the groceries here anyway?

segments.speaker: Unknown Speaker
segments.words: Yeah, I'll bring them over when they come.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: She's... she's helping me out. Yeah, well, it wasn't the same crew. It was different crews, you know, down there in Portland. I was with a bunch of... I remember my cousin. A bunch of others from different places, you know. Not very far from the hometown, but... 60 miles, I think. And I get... you know, when you talk the language, where you can get... ...to do the first thing.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you... if you would go back to work on the... On the railroad, you wouldn't go back to the same old crew you were on before?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No… not down there in Portland. I mean, they weren't... Well, the crew split, you see, from... From down there to ... They took us down to..… ...Chehalis… and... We worked while there. They were putting in double trudge. At that time. And it was in the wintertime, and it was more... more... it was terrible… so..… we worked a while, and then... In the wintertime... They got pretty muddy, you know, and we quit a whole bunch… i was quick… and I went to Portland. That's when I went to... This construction works. That was in 1911… and..… from one construction to the other, and then I went back... Railroad. I worked on... I worked on a... Belt line, they call it. The Hood River, there is a little branch line... That goes up to..… the apple belt… it's up on the farms where there's... they grow the apples, you know. They grow a lot of apples in...

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Hood River, there. Hood River grow apples there, they would know it… for the..… wenatchee, isn't it?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: But more so in Hood River, they... it's... Apple belt, I think, was called the little line. I worked on that there for a while.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were you just going to where the best money was and the best job you could find?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, the only job at that time, it was... that was the only job, you see. And some fella found the work, you know, and he needed a couple more men… and..… myself and my cousin went over, two cousins. I had from Portland. And I had two cousins from... They were in Silverton, Oregon for many, many years. They died now. One was married. And had three boys, I think. Two boys with his first wife. And one boy with a second. He was married two times… pretty good man… but he died here and he was younger man, ...? He's called his brother. There's two brothers. His brother died before him and he was the oldest. And I worked there too in Silverton… on Redwood… that was Logan Road. It wasn't much of a railroad but they were hauling logs, that's all. For the Silver Falls Timber Company… the mill… the mill was in Silverton. They had some big logs in these.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was your job there?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: On the railroad.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were you saving money on all these different jobs or were you sort of just spending it as you made it?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: You could save very much. Because you worked, you know. You worked for a while and then you quit and you go down and you stay there for a while and you would like to spend money in town. And then you did another job. Well, I did save a little bit. Enough to send my father back to Elk River because he was too old to work.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was the working?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: I gave him somebody who he left. Because he couldn't pay, you know. $400, I don't know, $400 was a lot of money in those days. And all I had, that's all I had, you see. I gave it to him too. What do you want for me?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you made money, you had money like that. Did you just keep it with you? All that money?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yes. Yes… while I was traveling, now if I went to Poland, I put it in a bank. But when I was traveling from one place to the other, I kept it with me. And of course, when I came to Spokane, I... Let's see… no… i came to Badlads in 1914 from the railroad. The branch line of the Hapner Junction, you know what Hapner is? I worked over there for quite a while at Hapner, and then they laid us off. I and my brother. And then I had three calls in share. They were a lot of them. They all called for me. Seven in town, but those were the calls, you see. And I kept corresponding with them, and they said, come on. So I came from Hapner Junction. I came to Colfax. And from Colfax to Moscow on one coach. One coach, it was from Colfax to Moscow. I don't remember what that one coach was for, but that's all there was, just one coach. Then it was its own machine, you see. It was run by electricity. I came to Badlads to Palouse from Moscow on Electric 10. At that time, I think it was the Roman Electric line from Moscow to Spokane.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: I don't remember what that was.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was that the Inland Electric or the Spokane?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yeah, I think it was the Inland. I think it was the Inland. I don't remember. But anyway, we came in Palouse and from Palouse. At that time, they were running through from here to Palouse to Bovill. You see, Washington, Idaho and Montana, this railroad here, they intended, when they built that, to run into Montana, but they didn't. They went up to, as far as Bovill, and then they connected to the Milwaukee. Because the Milwaukee came from East over there to St. Mary's and then from St. Mary's to Bovill, and they didn't have to build their own lines. And there were a lot of stockholders, you know, that they owned the Milwaukee. And that's why they called this side of Washington, right, of Atlanta.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I wanted to ask you about your father, too, when you were saying that he was, he got too old. Was the work over here hard on him because of his age?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Oh, yeah. It's really ... He couldn't work on the railroad. We had, when I was, so, I can't...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Just a moth.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: I can't see where it is, but it's flying inside, isn't it?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Just a moth, that's all. He's against the window.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No, he couldn't work. We had him as a war boy, you see, in a gang of men. And that's all he was doing, you see, he was carrying war. They had what they called war boys. 20, 30 men, you know. And he couldn't do any other work. It was too hard for him, so... There was a bunch of fellas going to Hulk Andre and he... He wrote me, he was here in Spokane, and I was in Portland that time. I was working in a white salmon in a dam. And I am giving money to go to your country. And that time was a war between the Malcolm States and Greece, you see… greece and Bulgaria… and there were a lot of young fellas, you know, from here they left. They went to war there. But I had sent the old man, they kid me, you know, when I called Martha to Spokane and said, you send your old man to fight in war, I said, yeah.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: And they went all together, you see, at a company… and he..… oh, it's been a pretty rough life, all right. But here in Potlatch, I settled here and I... I made level one here, but I went back to Greece in 1962, 1961. And I found my sister, the widow, and two kids. I was in pretty bad shape. And I had the help, I couldn't..… couldn't get away… so... now it's too late to make money. And the inflation took quite a bit. I had one house next to this here, that's where I was living before. And when I came back, I bought this one here. And cost me twice as much as it did to remodel it, you see, it was... inside was no..… nothing… and cost me twice as much as it cost me for that. There too, you see, because the wedges were high and the materials high. And I bought the car in Moscow. That cost me a couple thousand dollars and I can't drive it now, I have to sell it.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: If I can get anything out of it, I don't know. But... because it's... It's all, you know... fifty... fifty-nine model... You've seen it? Have you seen it?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Is it out front? Is it out in front?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No, no, it's in the garage. Okay, no, no. It's a Catalina.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You should be able to sell it?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yeah, Catalina, only thirty-five, thirty-six thousand miles. I don't know how to say much.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You should be able to sell it and get a good price if it's got low mileage like that.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, they're looking model, you see.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And if you're going to sell it to a garage, why they wouldn't give you nothing?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No, sell it to a person. They wouldn't give you nothing anyway. I don't know what it's worth now because it's pretty old money. Did...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: had your father been here very long before he went back to the old country?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Yes, he's been here before... before I was used... he came here in nineteen-seven and left in nineteen-twelve. Seventy-twelve is five years.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Could he work when he first came over pretty good?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Not very well. But he could get by, you know, with other men. All the same town, you see. They were..… and..… he got worse, you know, as a... you know, he got... He got all... I don't remember how old he was… but..… back in old country, he never worked, you see. He had a little store there and he... He was a businessman.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What kind?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, tavern and... It's mixed there, you know, with several kinds of things. Few... clothing and... and so on and so forth, yeah. Do you know why... He decided to come here to make money, but...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, that's it, to make money?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: He found that money is not easy, he is not grown in the trees. You see, you gotta work here. Did you think a lot of people thought that same thing, they could come over...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: and just make money easy?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Just come over and make money and go ahead and go back. That's what I thought. But when I came here, I found out different. And I decided that I will never go back anywhere. But I did go back on vision. And it cost me plenty. But... In the last... In the last, you know... last call... I lived... if I lived two, three, or more years, why... that's all. And if I go blind, I don't know what I'm going to do with that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What do you mean if you live two, three more years?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: That's all. Well..… 83 years old and 23 years, maybe 86. I didn't get too old to live any longer. Of course, I lived to be 90, 100. I saw one man, a poor fellow, a old teacher from Moscow. He was 104 years old. He came to... Boise, from Ohio… and..… well, of course, he had somebody with him. He didn't travel alone. Then went back when he was 100 years old and went back and lived four more years. And he died. He was a teacher. He used to tell us about the old times, you know, how the teachers, how they walk. Or not black dirt, you know, between Moscow and Colfax. They used to walk. They didn't have no automobiles, no... Not even... well, they had the buggies. But he didn't have one and he had to walk. And the government sent him to... Hawaii... to teach English. But he didn't like it. He came back and he went back to Ohio. I don't know how he called me. I went to Ohio. But he was a little bit more than I thought. That's why he died. Pretty nice, we'll follow.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you think, Gus, that people had a very good chance to really get ahead and get ahead quite a bit? Or was it hard?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Some people… some people, by working, you can't get ahead, you see. It just makes living a toll. If you're in a business, you might get ahead. One fella, a Greek fella, he wasn't educated or anything. But he went to... From here he went to Spokane and he got in a business there, in that clubhouse there. And he lost what he had. He went back to work in the Summerfield and made a few dollars and went to Seattle. And got into a partnership with another fella there. There was one place there that was ready to burst, you see. And he went in there. And he was lucky that the war started at the same time and he got out there with $100 ,000, believe it or not. I saw it with my own eyes. And he wasn't smart or anything, but he just headed for the business. Because by working you can't make the money. You have to save it.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Save it in England and still you don't get ahead. But there are a lot of fellas, a lot of Greek fellas that are doing business and they made money, others lost.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Is it just luck that makes a person win or lose?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: Well, I think so. Of course you have to have experience in business. But that fella didn't have nothing, no experience, but he was pretty tight with his money and he made it. And he went back to Greece and got married and he came to New York and I don't know what happened from there on. And here he bought a apartment house over there. You know, a apartment house was getting a lot of guys that were known from the war country and others. It was a regular apartment house for anybody. And of course his wife was helped. And I don't know what happened. I haven't lost the trash of him, I haven't read or anything.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would a little bit of money in the United States go a long ways in Greece for men to go back?

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: No, not now. No, I mean in the early days. In the early days, yes. But now everything is the same. You buy one pair of pants or one suit of clothes, you may have to pay a little cheaper but not very much. Because everything over there now is based on the dollar, on the price. Of the dollar. And they don't manufacture anything there anyway and all comes in either from England or France or United States. And they can't afford to sell it any cheaper because they sell it here because they have to pay the price to buy it. And now it's the dollar, it's the best of all occurrences in Europe. And especially in the southern Europe. Because Greece is a small country, you know, it's not... I don't produce anything, they have to import most everything and they have no export. They don't have nothing to sell in exchange, you know.

segments.speaker: Gus Demus
segments.words: But..… at first, years ago, they used to have something, they had what they call the..… the raisins… the raisins there. Before they started raising in California. The raisins from Greece, you see. And they sold them to the United States and they were getting money, they were getting a pretty good price. And now, they raised everything in California. Raises, olive oil, olives and things, you know, that they raised over there. And they don't get nothing here because California raises everything.

metadata.description: Laboring in the Northwest: language barrier, foreman-crew relations. Sending father back to Greece. Ten hour day at Potlatch. IWW radicalism. Getting ahead in America. 9-12-75 2 hr 33p
